title: Recount Writing
summary: How to retell real events for Paper 1: what a recount is, features, the five-paragraph structure, phrases for every part, vocabulary, a strong sample and practice.

blocks.text: A **recount** retells **real events that have already happened**, usually in the order they happened (chronological order). Most recounts in the exam are **personal recounts**: you write about something that happened to you, in the first person and the past tense, with your thoughts, feelings and a reflection at the end. A recount can also be **factual** (for example, a report of a school trip for the newsletter), but it still follows time order.

rows: To retell events so the reader understands what happened, and often to entertain them and share how you felt.
Classmates, teachers, parents, readers of a school blog, magazine or display.
Usually first person (I, we) for a personal recount. Third person for a factual recount of an event.
Past tense: I walked, we were waiting, it had started.

Paper 1 (Non-fiction), Section B Writing, 25 marks, about 30 minutes. Recount tasks often do not use the word 'recount'. Look for: 'write about a time when…', 'describe what happened', 'tell the reader about a day…', 'write an account of…'. Recount skills are also used inside diaries, letters to friends, blogs and news reports.
One event, in order, with a reflection
A plot with a problem and a resolution

blocks.text: What earns marks in a recount

headers: What a top answer looks like in a recount
rows: Every bullet covered. The setting is clear, the events are interesting and detailed, feelings are shown, and the ending reflects on what the day meant.
Vivid verbs (wandered, dashed, spotted), strong feeling words (relieved, terrified, elated) and some sensory detail.
Orientation → events in order → reflective conclusion. Time connectives at the start of paragraphs. Paragraphs change with time or place.
Past tenses used correctly (including 'was walking' and 'had left'). Varied sentence openings and lengths. Direct speech punctuated correctly.
Past-tense spellings correct (stopped, carried, realised) and ambitious words spelt correctly.
Last winter, my family and I went to the Cairo International Book Fair.
First… → When I turned round… → Ten minutes later… → Looking back…
First, · After that, · Suddenly, · Then, · Later, · In the end,
I spotted a stall and wandered over to it.
The huge halls were packed with families.
My heart was racing, and every voice sounded like a stranger's.
I had saved my pocket money for three months.
'If you get lost, find someone in a uniform.'
Looking back, I realise that the day taught me two lessons.

blocks.text: The teacher uses the **five-paragraph** recount: one orientation paragraph, three paragraphs of events in time order, and one conclusion. Start each event paragraph with a time connective, and make the middle event (the most exciting or important moment) your most detailed paragraph.

rows: A short title that hints at what happened
'The Day the Bus Broke Down', 'Lost at the Book Fair'
Who, where, when and why you were there. Set the scene with one or two details.
Hook the reader: 'It all started on a cold Friday morning…'
What happened first. How you felt.
The most important, surprising or exciting part
Slow it down: senses, feelings, a short sentence for drama.
How the situation developed or was solved
A short line of speech can bring it to life.
How it ended + what you think or feel about it now, what you learned
Use 'Looking back, …' or 'That day taught me…'. Link back to the title.

blocks.title: Do not just list events
blocks.text: Weak: "We went to the museum. Then we saw a mummy. Then we had lunch. Then we went home." Strong: "As soon as we entered the dark hall, the room fell silent. In a glass case lay a mummy, wrapped in yellowing cloth, and I could hardly believe it was more than three thousand years old." Choose fewer events and give each one detail and feeling.

groups.title: How to start (orientation)
items: The day began like any other, but things soon took an unexpected turn.
I remember clearly that it was a [day/time] when…
I could never have imagined what was about to happen.

groups.title: Events (body)
items: As I was [doing something], I noticed…
At that moment, I thought to myself…
Things took a dramatic turn when…

groups.title: Showing feelings
items: A wave of relief washed over me.
I felt my face turn bright red.

groups.title: How to end (conclusion and reflection)
items: That day taught me an important lesson about…
I will never forget how I felt when…
What I took away from that day was…
Although it was frightening at the time, I am glad it happened, because…
full of interesting happenings: an eventful journey
the excited feeling of waiting for something
a short trip for pleasure or learning
to see something for a very short time
to walk slowly without a plan

blocks.title: Sample: 'Lost at the Book Fair'
blocks.task: Your class is making a display called 'A Day I Will Never Forget'. Write about a day when something did not go as planned. Think about: • where you were and who you were with • what happened, in order • how you felt • what you learned.
text: Last winter, my family and I went to the Cairo International Book Fair. It was a cold, sunny Friday, and the huge halls were packed with families, school groups and endless tables of books. I had saved my pocket money for three months, and I was determined to buy the whole adventure series I had been dreaming about.

First, we visited the children's hall, where colourful posters covered every wall. My dad told me to stay close, but I was too excited to listen. While he was paying for my sister's colouring books, I spotted a stall with the series I wanted. Without thinking, I wandered over to look at it.

When I turned round, my family had disappeared. Suddenly, the crowd felt enormous. My heart was racing, my hands were sweating and every voice sounded like a stranger's. I walked up and down the rows, but each one looked exactly the same. For one terrible moment, I wanted to cry.

Then I remembered what my mum always says: 'If you get lost, find someone in a uniform.' I took a deep breath and walked to a security guard near the entrance. He smiled kindly, asked for my name and spoke into his radio. Ten minutes later, which felt like ten hours, my dad came running towards me. He hugged me so tightly that I could hardly breathe.

Looking back, I realise that the day taught me two important lessons. Firstly, it is easy to forget the rules when you are excited. Secondly, staying calm is the fastest way out of trouble. I did buy my books in the end, but I read the first one sitting very close to my dad!
blocks.marks: Strong answer: Creation 5/5 · Vocabulary 3/3 · Structure 7/7 · Grammar & punctuation 7/7 · Spelling 3/3
notes: Format decision: the task did not name a format (no 'diary', no 'letter'), so this is a normal recount: a title and five paragraphs, with no date line and no greeting.

Creation of texts 5/5: all four bullets are covered: where and who (P1), what happened in order (P2–P4), feelings all the way through (excited, racing heart, wanting to cry, relief in the hug), what I learned (P5). The reader is kept interested by a clear problem (getting lost) and a satisfying solution.

Recount features: orientation with who/where/when/why (P1), strict time order, time connectives at the start of paragraphs ('Last winter', 'First', 'When I turned round', 'Then', 'Looking back') and inside them ('Without thinking', 'Ten minutes later'), past tense, first person, factual details (three months of pocket money), one line of remembered speech and a reflective ending.

Vocabulary and language 3/3: vivid verbs ('spotted', 'wandered', 'hugged'), feeling words ('determined', 'terrible'), sensory detail ('colourful posters', 'packed with families') and exaggeration for effect ('felt like ten hours').

Structure of texts 7/7: the teacher's five-paragraph recount: orientation → event 1 (getting separated) → event 2, the main moment, slowed down (lost) → event 3 (the solution) → reflection. The final sentence links back to the books from P1 and ends with a light, humorous touch.

Grammar and punctuation 7/7: a range of past tenses ('went', 'was paying', 'had disappeared', 'had been dreaming') · varied sentences (the short 'Suddenly, the crowd felt enormous.' after a calm paragraph) · a colon to introduce the mother's words · a pair of commas for extra information ('Ten minutes later, which felt like ten hours,') · commas after fronted adverbials · a list of three with commas · apostrophes for possession ('children's', 'sister's', 'stranger's').

items: Listing events with 'and then… and then…' and no detail or feeling.
Telling every small thing (waking up, brushing teeth, breakfast) and running out of time before the important moment.
No orientation: the reader does not know where or when it happened.
Slipping into the present tense ('I walk to the stall and I see…').
Writing a long conversation. Use one or two short lines of speech only.
Ending with 'And then I went home and went to sleep.' instead of a reflection.
Adding 'Dear Diary' or a date when the task did not ask for a diary.
Forgetting a bullet point, usually 'what you learned'.

blocks.title: Recount checklist
items: Title that hints at what happened.
P1 orientation: who, where, when, why.
Three event paragraphs in time order, each starting with a time connective.
The main moment is slowed down with senses and feelings.
Past tense all the way through (present only in the reflection, for what is true now).
One or two short lines of speech, correctly punctuated (optional).
P5: how it ended + what I learned, linked back to the title.
Checked: full stops, commas after time connectives, spelling of past-tense verbs.

blocks.title: كيف تكتب Recount ممتازاً
blocks.text: الـ Recount هو حكاية أحداث حقيقية حدثت بالفعل، بالترتيب، وبصيغة الماضي. استخدم خمس فقرات: (1) مقدمة: مَن، أين، متى، ولماذا (2) و(3) و(4) الأحداث بالترتيب، وكل فقرة تبدأ بكلمة زمنية مثل First أو Suddenly أو Later (5) خاتمة: كيف انتهى اليوم وماذا تعلمت. لا تكتب كل التفاصيل الصغيرة، بل اختر لحظة مهمة واحكها ببطء مع مشاعرك.

rows: G.A.A.P. + plan: title, five boxes, a feeling and a detail for each event
P2–P4 events (spend longest on the main moment)
Check tenses, time connectives, punctuation of speech, spelling

items.q: Practice: "Write an account of a school trip or a family outing that you enjoyed, for your class blog. Consider: • where you went and why • the most interesting part • something that surprised you • what you will remember most." Write a short plan.
items.a: G.A.A.P.: recount for a blog (title, past tense, time order, first person, friendly tone) · audience = classmates and parents → friendly but correct · 'Consider' → at least 3 bullets, use all 4 · purpose = recount + entertain. Title: 'A Morning with the Pharaohs'. P1 Orientation: Year 6 trip to the Grand Egyptian Museum, why (our history topic), the early bus, excitement. P2 Arrival: the giant statue in the entrance hall, how small I felt. P3 Most interesting part (slowed down): the hall of treasures, gold shining, guide's facts, my notes. P4 Surprise: the guide let us try writing our names in hieroglyphs · mine had a bird and a lion. P5 What I will remember: the feeling of standing in front of something 3,000 years old · lesson: history is not just in books. Link back to the title.

items.q: Improve this recount opening: "I went to the beach. It was good."
items.a: "Last August, my cousins and I spent a whole day at Ain Sokhna beach. The sea was a bright, glittering blue, and the sand was so hot that we had to run to the water. None of us knew that, by the end of the day, we would be heroes." (who/where/when + description + a hook)

items.q: Put these time connectives in a sensible order for a recount: Finally · First · Suddenly · After that · Looking back
items.a: First → After that → Suddenly → Finally → Looking back (the last one starts the reflection).
